First look at the data: animal disease outbreaks and weather¶

Project: WOAH Datathon, Topic 6 - trends in animal disease occurrence.

This notebook is a guided tour of every dataset the pipeline has built. It does not model anything. For each dataset you get: what one row means, its size, the first rows, summary statistics and the share of missing values. After the tables come simple charts, each with a "what to look at" line and a one-line takeaway.

Words you will meet

Word Plain meaning
WAHIS WOAH's World Animal Health Information System - where countries report disease to WOAH.
Outbreak One disease occurrence at one place (a farm, a village, a wild-bird site) with a start date.
Event One disease episode in one country. It groups many outbreaks (e.g. an African swine fever wave in Poland).
Report lag Days between an outbreak starting and it being reported.
Grid cell A square of the WorldClim weather map (about 18 km wide). Each outbreak is matched to one cell.
Anomaly detector Compares each month's outbreak count with what the previous five years predicted (ignoring past one-off waves), and flags months far above that.

Contents: 1 outbreaks - 2 events - 3 outbreak-to-cell lookup - 4 climate - 5 detector results - 6 report tables - 7 charts on disease records - 8 charts on weather - 9 charts on the detector (including baseline vs autoregressive) - 10 things to know.

Every chart is also saved as a PNG file in the charts/ folder at the project root.

import warnings
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from IPython.display import Markdown, display
from matplotlib.ticker import FuncFormatter, MaxNLocator
from scipy.stats import norm

sys.path.insert(
    0, str(Path.cwd().parent)
)  # project root, so we can import the t6 package
from t6 import config as C
from t6.series import merge_diseases, score_end

warnings.filterwarnings(

pd.set_option("display.max_columns", None)
pd.set_option("display.width", 220)
pd.set_option("display.float_format", "{:,.2f}".format)

# ---- chart style: quiet greys + a colour-blind-safe palette -----------------
INK, INK2, MUTED, GRID, SURFACE = "#0b0b0b", "#52514e", "#898781", "#e1e0d9", "#fcfcfb"
BLUE, ORANGE, AQUA, RED = "#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#1baf7a", "#d03b3b"
BLUE_LIGHT, ORANGE_LIGHT = (
    "#9ec5f4",
    "#f6b79e",
)  # lighter tints = "partial / incomplete" data

plt.rcParams.update(
    {
        "figure.facecolor": SURFACE,
        "axes.facecolor": SURFACE,
        "savefig.facecolor": SURFACE,
        "figure.dpi": 100,
        "font.size": 10,
        "text.color": INK,
        "axes.labelcolor": INK2,

        "ytick.color": MUTED,
        "axes.edgecolor": "#c3c2b7",

        "axes.grid": True,

        "axes.titlelocation": "left",

# one colour per region, used on every chart. Only three hues stay distinguishable on a
# map, so the two small regions (Americas, Middle East) share a neutral grey.
REGION_COLOR = {
    "Europe": BLUE,
    "Asia and the Pacific": ORANGE,
    "Africa": AQUA,
    "Americas": MUTED,
    "Middle East": MUTED,
    "Other": MUTED,
}

thousands = FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:,.0f}")

# every chart is also saved as an image file in <project root>/charts/
CHARTS = C.ROOT / "charts"
CHARTS.mkdir(exist_ok=True)


def save_chart(fig, name):
    fig.savefig(
        CHARTS / name, dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight", facecolor=fig.get_facecolor()
    )


def null_share(df):
    """Show the % of missing values for the columns that have any."""
    s = df.isna().mean().mul(100)
    s = s[s > 0].sort_values(ascending=False)
    if s.empty:
        print("No missing values in any column.")
    else:
        display(s.rename("% missing").to_frame())


def describe_all(df):
    """describe() for every column (numbers, dates and text), one row per column."""
    return df.describe(include="all").T

Load the data¶

All files are read from data/interim/ (cleaned tables) and data/processed/ (detector output). The big weather table (13.9 million rows) is loaded once; charts later pick out single grid cells from it.

1. outbreaks - one row per outbreak¶

One row is one outbreak reported to WAHIS (immediate notifications and their follow-up reports), January 2005 to July 2026: which disease, where (country and coordinates), when it started, when it was reported, and how many animals were affected. Key columns: Outbreak_id, epi_event_id (the event it belongs to), disease, iso_code/country/region, Outbreak_start_date, start_month, Reporting_date, report_lag_days, Latitude/Longitude, Location_approx (True when the coordinates are only approximate), Is_cluster, cases, dead, susceptible, n_species.

last_ok = score_end()  # newest month the pipeline treats as complete
checks = {
    "Duplicate Outbreak_id": ob["Outbreak_id"].duplicated().sum(),
    "Reported BEFORE it started (negative lag)": (ob["report_lag_days"] < 0).sum(),
    "Reported more than a year after it started": (ob["report_lag_days"] > 365).sum(),
    "End date earlier than start date": (
        ob["Outbreak_end_date"] < ob["Outbreak_start_date"]
    ).sum(),
    "No end date (still ongoing or never closed)": ob["Outbreak_end_date"].isna().sum(),
    "Coordinates only approximate (Location_approx)": ob["Location_approx"].sum(),
    "cases = 0": (ob["cases"] == 0).sum(),
    "dead larger than cases": (ob["dead"] > ob["cases"]).sum(),
    "susceptible = 0 (probably 'not reported')": (ob["susceptible"] == 0).sum(),
    "Region = Other (Antarctica)": (ob["region"] == "Other").sum(),
    "Same disease + coordinates + start date as another row": ob.duplicated(
        ["disease", "Latitude", "Longitude", "Outbreak_start_date"]
    ).sum(),
    f"Started after {last_ok:%Y-%m} (newest months, still incomplete)": (
        ob["start_month"] > last_ok
    ).sum(),
}
out = pd.DataFrame({"rows": pd.Series(checks)})
out["% of all outbreaks"] = out["rows"] / len(ob) * 100
out.style.format({"rows": "{:,.0f}", "% of all outbreaks": "{:.2f}%"})

2. events - one row per epidemiological event¶

One row is one event: a disease occurring in a country, which then contains many outbreaks. reason_for_notification says why it was reported (e.g. "First occ in country" = first ever in that country, "reccurence disease" [sic] = it came back). n_outbreaks and n_reports count what the event contains.

4. cell_climate - monthly weather for every grid cell with outbreaks¶

One row is one grid cell in one month (1990 to 2024): tmin/tmax are the lowest and highest daily temperature averages (deg C), prec is rainfall (mm). The three anomaly columns say how unusual that month was for that cell compared with the 1991-2020 average of the same calendar month: tmin_anom/tmax_anom in deg C, prec_z as a z-score (0 = normal, +2 = unusually wet), capped at +/-5. This table is large (about 500 MB), so describe() takes a few seconds and charts use one cell at a time.

5. tests_outbreaks and tests_events - anomaly detector results¶

One row is one monthly check of one series. A series is a disease in an area: the whole world (level = global), one WOAH region, or one country. For every month the detector fits a baseline on the previous years (leaving out past one-off waves, so an old wave is not "expected" again) and asks: is this month's count unusually high?

  • y = observed count, mu = expected count from the baseline, upper99 = the count that would only be exceeded 1% of the time.
  • p, q = p-value and its false-discovery-rate adjusted version; ratio = y / mu; z = standardised residual (0 = as expected).
  • alert = True when the month is flagged as a real surge (rules just below).
  • status: tested (has a baseline), first_occurrence (disease never seen in that area before, nothing to compare with), reemergence (back after a long absence). Only tested rows have mu, p, upper99 and alerts - so those columns are missing on the other rows.
  • period: retrospective up to Dec 2024 (weather available) and holdout after (kept aside to check the detector).
  • phi, se_eta, var are technical details of the baseline and can be ignored for now.

tests_outbreaks counts outbreaks per month; tests_events counts events per month (same columns, metric differs). A second variant, tests_outbreaks_ar1, also asks whether a month is a surprise given last month; it is compared with the baseline in 9.4.

In [23]:
display(
    Markdown(
        f"**Settings used** (from `t6/config.py`): the baseline looks back {C.WINDOW_MONTHS // 12} years ({C.WINDOW_MONTHS} months) and needs at least {C.MIN_WINDOW} months of history. "
        f"A month is an **alert** when it is statistically well above expected (false-discovery rate {C.FDR_Q:.0%}), at least {C.MIN_ALERT_RATIO:g} times the expected count, "
        f"and at least {C.MIN_ALERT_COUNT['outbreaks']} outbreaks ({C.MIN_ALERT_COUNT['events']} events for the events table)."
    )
)

Settings used (from t6/config.py): the baseline looks back 5 years (60 months) and needs at least 24 months of history. A month is an alert when it is statistically well above expected (false-discovery rate 5%), at least 2 times the expected count, and at least 3 outbreaks (2 events for the events table).

6. Small report tables in reports/tables/¶

Two summaries written by the pipeline. calibration.csv (baseline) and calibration_ar1.csv (autoregressive variant) check whether the detector behaves as a fair test should (for a perfect test mean_z is about 0, sd_z about 1, frac_p<0.05 about 0.05 and frac_p<0.01 about 0.01). episodes_outbreaks.csv merges consecutive alert months of one series into a single episode with its peak size and excess outbreaks.

)

Charts¶

7. Disease records: how many, which diseases, where, how fast¶

7.1 Events and outbreaks per year¶

What to look at: how the bars grow from left to right. Left: new events per year; right: outbreaks per year (by start date). The pale 2026 bar is a partial year (data ends in July 2026).

In [36]:
def year_bars(ax, series, title, ylabel):
    years = series.index.to_numpy()
    colors = [BLUE_LIGHT if y == 2026 else BLUE for y in years]
    ax.bar(years, series.to_numpy(), color=colors, width=0.7)
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.set_ylabel(ylabel)
    ax.set_xlabel("Year (start date)")
    ax.set_xticks(years[::2])
    ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(thousands)


ev_year = ev.groupby(ev["start_month"].dt.year).size()
ob_year = ob.groupby(ob["start_month"].dt.year).size()

fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 3.8))
year_bars(a1, ev_year, "Events per year", "Events")
year_bars(a2, ob_year, "Outbreaks per year", "Outbreaks")
fig.tight_layout()
save_chart(fig, "7_1_events_and_outbreaks_per_year.png")
plt.show()

y0, y1 = ob_year.index.min(), ob_year.index.max() - 1  # first year and last full year
display(
    Markdown(
        f"**Takeaway:** reporting volume grows a lot: {ev_year[y0]:,} events and {ob_year[y0]:,} outbreaks in {y0} "
        f"versus {ev_year[y1]:,} events and {ob_year[y1]:,} outbreaks in {y1} "
        f"(x{ev_year[y1] / ev_year[y0]:.0f} and x{ob_year[y1] / ob_year[y0]:.0f}). "
        "Some of that is real disease spread (African swine fever, bird flu), some is more countries reporting more completely, "
        "so compare years with care."
    )
)

Takeaway: reporting volume grows a lot: 99 events and 1,137 outbreaks in 2005 versus 830 events and 28,608 outbreaks in 2025 (x8 and x25). Some of that is real disease spread (African swine fever, bird flu), some is more countries reporting more completely, so compare years with care.

7.2 Top 10 diseases and outbreaks by WOAH region¶

What to look at: the length of each bar. Left: the 10 diseases with the most outbreaks (the two bird-flu labels are combined into "HPAI (all hosts)", the same merge the detector uses). Right: outbreaks by WOAH region.

In [37]:
def hbar(ax, labels, values, colors, title, xlabel):
    y = np.arange(len(values))[::-1]
    ax.barh(y, values, color=colors, height=0.65)
    ax.set_yticks(y, labels)
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.set_xlabel(xlabel)
    ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
    ax.grid(axis="x")
    ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(thousands)
    ax.xaxis.set_major_locator(MaxNLocator(5))
    ax.set_xlim(0, max(values) * 1.15)
    for yi, v in zip(y, values):
        ax.text(v, yi, f" {v:,}", va="center", fontsize=9, color=INK2)


ob_m = ob.assign(
    disease=merge_diseases(ob["disease"])
)  # HPAI merge applied once, reused below
top_dis = ob_m["disease"].value_counts().head(10)
reg = ob["region"].value_counts()
reg = reg[reg.index != "Other"]  # 'Other' is 2 outbreaks in Antarctica

fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(
    1, 2, figsize=(14, 4.4), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.5, 1]}
)
hbar(
    a1,
    [textwrap.shorten(d, 46, placeholder="...") for d in top_dis.index],
    top_dis.to_numpy(),
    BLUE,
    "Top 10 diseases by outbreaks",
    "Outbreaks",
)
hbar(
    a2,
    reg.index,
    reg.to_numpy(),
    [REGION_COLOR[r] for r in reg.index],
    "Outbreaks by WOAH region",
    "Outbreaks",
)
fig.tight_layout()
save_chart(fig, "7_2_top_10_diseases_and_outbreaks_by_woah_region.png")
plt.show()

tot = len(ob)
top3 = top_dis.head(3)
display(
    Markdown(
        f"**Takeaway:** the top three diseases ({top3.index[0]}, {top3.index[1]} and {top3.index[2]}) make up {top3.sum() / tot:.0%} "
        f"of all outbreaks, and Europe supplies {reg['Europe'] / tot:.0%}. "
        'Any "global" trend is therefore largely a European story.'
    )
)

Takeaway: the top three diseases (African swine fever virus, HPAI (all hosts) and Bluetongue virus) make up 76% of all outbreaks, and Europe supplies 71%. Any "global" trend is therefore largely a European story.

7.3 Top 10 countries¶

What to look at: which countries report the most outbreaks.

In [38]:
top_c = ob["country"].value_counts().head(10)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.2))
hbar(
    ax,
    top_c.index,
    top_c.to_numpy(),
    BLUE,
    "Top 10 countries by outbreaks",
    "Outbreaks",
)
fig.tight_layout()
save_chart(fig, "7_3_top_10_countries.png")
plt.show()
n_eu = ob.groupby("country")["region"].first()[top_c.index].eq("Europe").sum()
print(
    f"These 10 countries hold {top_c.sum() / len(ob):.0%} of all outbreaks ({ob['country'].nunique()} countries in total); {n_eu} of the 10 are in Europe."
)

These 10 countries hold 54% of all outbreaks (190 countries in total); 8 of the 10 are in Europe.

Takeaway: the counts are concentrated in a few, mostly European, countries. A high count can reflect a big epidemic or thorough reporting, so it is not a risk ranking.

7.4 Where outbreaks are: a simple map¶

What to look at: each dot is one outbreak at its longitude/latitude, coloured by WOAH region (no coastline drawn). Dots are small and see-through, so darker areas have many overlapping outbreaks.

In [39]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 5.6))
order = [
    "Europe",
    "Asia and the Pacific",
    "Africa",
    "Americas",
    "Middle East",
]  # dense Europe goes underneath
for r in order:
    d = ob[ob["region"] == r]
    ax.scatter(
        d["Longitude"],
        d["Latitude"],
        s=3,
        alpha=0.3,
        linewidths=0,
        color=REGION_COLOR[r],
        rasterized=True,
    )
labels = {
    "Europe": "Europe",
    "Asia and the Pacific": "Asia and the Pacific",
    "Africa": "Africa",
    "Americas": "Americas and Middle East (grey)",
}
for name, col in zip(labels.values(), [BLUE, ORANGE, AQUA, MUTED]):
    ax.scatter([], [], s=40, color=col, label=name)
ax.legend(loc="lower left", bbox_to_anchor=(0.6, 0.0), frameon=False)
ax.set_xlim(-180, 180)
ax.set_ylim(-60, 85)
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.grid(True, axis="both")
ax.set_xlabel("Longitude")
ax.set_ylabel("Latitude")
ax.set_title("Outbreak locations")
save_chart(fig, "7_4_where_outbreaks_are_a_simple_map.png")
plt.show()
print(
    f"{ob['Location_approx'].mean():.0%} of outbreaks have only approximate coordinates (for example the centre of a district)."
)

20% of outbreaks have only approximate coordinates (for example the centre of a district).

Takeaway: coverage is very uneven. Europe is densely covered, and large parts of Africa, Central Asia and the Americas show few points, which means "no reports", not necessarily "no disease".

7.5 How long do reports take?¶

What to look at: the histogram of days between an outbreak starting and its report. The x-axis stops at 365 days; the two vertical lines mark the median (half of outbreaks are reported faster) and the 90th percentile (9 in 10 are reported faster).

In [40]:
lag = ob["report_lag_days"]
med, p90 = lag.median(), lag.quantile(0.9)
shown = lag[(lag >= 0) & (lag <= 365)]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4))
ax.hist(shown, bins=np.arange(0, 366, 5), color=BLUE)
top = ax.get_ylim()[1]
for v, name in ((med, "median"), (p90, "90th percentile")):
    ax.axvline(v, color=INK2, lw=1.2)
    ax.text(v + 4, top * 0.93, f"{name}: {v:.0f} days", color=INK, fontsize=10)
ax.set_xlim(0, 365)
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(thousands)
ax.set_xlabel("Days from outbreak start to report")
ax.set_ylabel("Outbreaks (5-day bins)")
ax.set_title("Reporting lag")
save_chart(fig, "7_5_how_long_do_reports_take.png")
plt.show()
print(
    f"Not shown: {(lag > 365).sum():,} outbreaks reported more than a year late (max {lag.max():,} days) "
    f"and {(lag < 0).sum():,} reported before their start date (min {lag.min():,} days)."
)

q = lag.quantile([0.5, 0.75, 0.9])
display(
    Markdown(
        f"**Takeaway:** half of outbreaks are reported within {q[0.5]:.0f} days and three quarters within {q[0.75]:.0f}, "
        f"but there is a long tail: 1 in 10 takes more than {q[0.9]:.0f} days (about {q[0.9] / 30.4:.0f} months). "
        f"That is why the newest months of any count are incomplete, and the pipeline ignores the last {C.CENSOR_MONTHS} months."
    )
)

Not shown: 2,188 outbreaks reported more than a year late (max 2,120 days) and 296 reported before their start date (min -849 days).

Takeaway: half of outbreaks are reported within 15 days and three quarters within 37, but there is a long tail: 1 in 10 takes more than 104 days (about 3 months). That is why the newest months of any count are incomplete, and the pipeline ignores the last 4 months.

7.6 Monthly outbreaks over time for three diseases¶

What to look at: the shape of each line. Each panel has its own y-axis scale, so compare shapes, not heights. The grey strip on the right marks recent months whose reports are still arriving.

In [41]:
focus = ["African swine fever virus", "Bluetongue virus", "HPAI (all hosts)"]
idx = pd.date_range("2005-01-01", "2026-06-01", freq="MS")
monthly = (
    ob_m[ob_m["disease"].isin(focus)]
    .groupby(["start_month", "disease"])
    .size()
    .unstack("disease", fill_value=0)
    .reindex(idx, fill_value=0)
)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(11, 8), sharex=True)
for ax, name in zip(axes, focus):
    s = monthly[name]
    ax.fill_between(s.index, s, color=BLUE, alpha=0.15, lw=0)
    ax.plot(s.index, s, color=BLUE, lw=1.4)
    ax.axvspan(
        last_ok + pd.Timedelta(days=15),
        idx[-1] + pd.Timedelta(days=30),
        color=MUTED,
        alpha=0.2,
        lw=0,
    )
    ax.set_title(f"{name}  ({s.sum():,} outbreaks)")
    ax.set_ylabel("Outbreaks per month")
    ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(thousands)
axes[0].text(
    last_ok + pd.Timedelta(days=25),
    axes[0].get_ylim()[1] * 0.95,
    "incomplete",
    ha="right",
    va="top",
    fontsize=9,
    color=INK2,
)
axes[-1].set_xlabel("Month of outbreak start")
fig.tight_layout()
save_chart(fig, "7_6_monthly_outbreaks_over_time_for_three_diseases.png")
plt.show()

Takeaway: the three diseases behave very differently: African swine fever climbed from 2014 and has stayed high (peaks in 2020, 2023 and 2025-26), bluetongue is a few huge waves (2007, 2014) between quiet years, and bird flu (HPAI) peaks in the northern winters, with recent ones the biggest.

8. Weather charts¶

8.1 One grid cell: temperature and rain, 2005-2024¶

What to look at: the cell with the most outbreaks. Left: its monthly highest temperature (orange line) and rainfall (blue bars) over time. Right: the same two measures averaged by calendar month (1991-2020), which is the "normal" year the anomaly columns are measured against.

In [42]:
top_cell = oc["cell_id"].value_counts().idxmax()
in_cell = ob.merge(oc, on="Outbreak_id").query("cell_id == @top_cell")
print(
    f"Cell {top_cell}: {len(in_cell):,} outbreaks, mostly in {in_cell['country'].mode()[0]} "
    f"(around lat {in_cell['Latitude'].mean():.1f}, lon {in_cell['Longitude'].mean():.1f}); "
    f"main diseases: {', '.join(merge_diseases(in_cell['disease']).value_counts().head(3).index)}"
)

c = cc[cc["cell_id"] == top_cell].set_index("month").sort_index()
ref = c.loc["1991":"2020"]
seasonal = ref.groupby(ref.index.month)[["tmax", "prec"]].mean()
win = c.loc["2005":"2024"]
mnames = ["J", "F", "M", "A", "M", "J", "J", "A", "S", "O", "N", "D"]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(
    2, 2, figsize=(12, 6), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [3, 1.2]}, sharex="col"
)
ax[0, 0].plot(win.index, win["tmax"], color=ORANGE, lw=1.4)
ax[0, 0].set_ylabel("Highest temperature (deg C)")
ax[0, 0].set_title("Monthly temperature, 2005-2024")
ax[1, 0].bar(win.index, win["prec"], width=25, color=BLUE)
ax[1, 0].set_ylabel("Rainfall (mm)")
ax[1, 0].set_title("Monthly rainfall, 2005-2024")
ax[1, 0].set_xlabel("Month")
ax[0, 1].plot(range(1, 13), seasonal["tmax"], color=ORANGE, lw=2, marker="o", ms=4)
ax[0, 1].set_title("Typical year")
ax[1, 1].bar(range(1, 13), seasonal["prec"], color=BLUE, width=0.7)
ax[1, 1].set_xticks(range(1, 13), mnames)
ax[1, 1].set_xlabel("Calendar month")
ax[0, 1].set_title("Average year (1991-2020)")
ax[1, 1].set_ylabel("")
fig.suptitle(
    f"Grid cell {top_cell} ({in_cell['country'].mode()[0]}, the cell with the most outbreaks)",
    x=0.01,
    ha="left",
    fontsize=13,
    fontweight="bold",
)
fig.tight_layout()
save_chart(fig, "8_1_one_grid_cell_temperature_and_rain_2005_2024.png")
plt.show()

Cell 523851: 608 outbreaks, mostly in Germany (around lat 49.6, lon 8.6); main diseases: African swine fever virus, HPAI (all hosts), West Nile Fever

Takeaway: weather is strongly seasonal, so raw temperature and rain mostly tell you the time of year. That is why the pipeline uses anomalies (departure from the normal for that calendar month) to see whether unusual weather is linked to disease.

8.2 The rainfall anomaly (prec_z) after capping¶

What to look at: how many cell-months have each prec_z value. Left: normal scale. Right: the same data on a log scale, so the thin tails are visible. The edges at -5 and +5 are where extreme values were capped.

In [43]:
counts, edges = np.histogram(cc["prec_z"].to_numpy(), bins=np.linspace(-5, 5, 101))
fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 3.8))
for ax, log in ((a1, False), (a2, True)):
    ax.bar(edges[:-1], counts / 1e6, width=np.diff(edges), align="edge", color=BLUE)
    ax.set_xlim(-5.3, 5.3)
    ax.set_xlabel("prec_z (0 = normal rainfall for that month)")
    ax.set_ylabel("Cell-months (millions)")
    if log:
        ax.set_yscale("log")
        ax.set_title("Same, log scale (shows the tails)")
    else:
        ax.set_title("Rainfall anomaly (prec_z)")
fig.tight_layout()
save_chart(fig, "8_2_the_rainfall_anomaly_prec_z_after_capping.png")
plt.show()
pz = cc["prec_z"]
skew = pz.skew()
display(
    Markdown(
        f"**Takeaway:** the anomaly is centred near 0 (mean {pz.mean():.2f}) with a spread of {pz.std():.2f}, as a z-score should be. "
        f"It is skewed to the {'wet' if skew > 0 else 'dry'} side (a few very {'wet' if skew > 0 else 'dry'} months) "
        f"and has a spike at exactly 0 ({(pz == 0).mean():.1%} of values) from desert cells where rain never varies in a given calendar month. "
        f"Nothing exceeds +/-{pz.abs().max():.0f} because of the cap, which touched only {(pz.abs() >= 5).mean():.3%} of values."
    )
)

Takeaway: the anomaly is centred near 0 (mean 0.00) with a spread of 0.98, as a z-score should be. It is skewed to the wet side (a few very wet months) and has a spike at exactly 0 (1.5% of values) from desert cells where rain never varies in a given calendar month. Nothing exceeds +/-5 because of the cap, which touched only 0.016% of values.

9. Detector charts¶

9.1 Two example series¶

What to look at: blue bars are the real monthly outbreak counts; the grey line is what the baseline expected; the grey band reaches up to the 99% upper bound. A red dot marks a month flagged as an alert. The first two years of each series are blank because the detector needs 24 months of history. The dotted line marks the start of the 2025+ holdout period. The y-axis stops just above the biggest observed count, so a very wide band can be cut off at the top.

In [44]:
tt = to[to["status"] == "tested"]


def get_series(level, area, disease):
    s = tt[(tt["level"] == level) & (tt["area"] == area) & (tt["disease"] == disease)]
    return s.sort_values("month").set_index("month")


def plot_detector(ax, s, title):
    ax.bar(s.index, s["y"], width=28, color=BLUE, label="Observed outbreaks")
    ax.fill_between(
        s.index,
        s["mu"],
        s["upper99"],
        color=MUTED,
        alpha=0.3,
        lw=0,
        label="Expected range (up to 99% upper bound)",
    )
    ax.plot(s.index, s["mu"], color=INK2, lw=1.5, label="Expected")
    a = s[s["alert"]]
    ax.scatter(
        a.index,
        a["y"],
        s=55,
        color=RED,
        edgecolor=SURFACE,
        linewidth=1.5,
        zorder=5,
        label=f"Alert ({len(a)} months)",
    )
    ax.axvline(pd.Timestamp(C.HOLDOUT_START), color=MUTED, lw=1, ls=":")
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.set_ylabel("Outbreaks per month")
    ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(thousands)
    ax.set_ylim(0, max(s["y"].max(), 1) * 1.25)
    ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=9)


fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(11, 8), sharex=True)
plot_detector(
    axes[0],
    get_series("global", "all", "Bluetongue virus"),
    "Bluetongue virus - whole world",
)
plot_detector(
    axes[1],
    get_series("region", "Europe", "HPAI (all hosts)"),
    "Bird flu (HPAI, all hosts) - Europe",
)
axes[1].set_xlabel("Month")
fig.tight_layout()
save_chart(fig, "9_1_two_example_series.png")
plt.show()


def alert_runs(s):
    # runs of consecutive alert months in one series
    m = s.index[s["alert"]]
    grp = (
        np.cumsum(np.r_[True, np.diff(m.year * 12 + m.month) != 1])
        if len(m)
        else np.array([], dtype=int)
    )
    return (
        pd.Series(m, index=m)
        .groupby(grp)
        .agg(first="first", last="last", months="size")
    )


lines = []
for name, s in (
    ("bluetongue (world)", get_series("global", "all", "Bluetongue virus")),
    ("bird flu (Europe)", get_series("region", "Europe", "HPAI (all hosts)")),
):
    r = alert_runs(s)
    big = r.sort_values("months", ascending=False).iloc[0]
    lines.append(
        f"{name}: {s['alert'].sum()} alert months in {len(r)} runs, the longest {big['months']} months "
        f"({big['first']:%b %Y} to {big['last']:%b %Y})"
    )
display(
    Markdown(
        "**Takeaway:** the detector flags the big surprises, and a big wave stays flagged for several months in a row: "
        + "; ".join(lines)
        + ". "
        "Bars far above the grey band are real surges; red dots on tiny counts (a few outbreaks where almost none were expected) are weaker signals."
    )
)

Takeaway: the detector flags the big surprises, and a big wave stays flagged for several months in a row: bluetongue (world): 33 alert months in 10 runs, the longest 8 months (May 2024 to Dec 2024); bird flu (Europe): 31 alert months in 12 runs, the longest 7 months (Nov 2016 to May 2017). Bars far above the grey band are real surges; red dots on tiny counts (a few outbreaks where almost none were expected) are weaker signals.

9.2 Alerts per year¶

What to look at: left, the number of alert months per year over all series; right, the same as a rate per 1,000 months tested (so years with more series being tested are not favoured). The pale bar is 2026 (partial year).

f0, f1 = rate.index.min(), rate.index.max()
cb = calib.query(

        f"The count grows from {yr.loc[f0, 'alerts']} in {f0} to {yr.loc[f1, 'alerts']} in {f1}, but so do the tests ({yr.loc[f0, 'tests']:,} to {yr.loc[f1, 'tests']:,}); "
        f"the rate per 1,000 tests ranges from {rate.min():.0f} to {rate.max():.0f} and is highest in {rate.idxmax()}. "

)

45,242 tested series-months, 2,210 alerts (4.88%).

Takeaway: about 1 in 20 tested months is flagged (4.9%), which is a lot of alerts to follow up. The count grows from 17 in 2007 to 252 in 2025, but so do the tests (436 to 3,444); the rate per 1,000 tests ranges from 17 to 73 and is highest in 2025. The detector is sensitive: 10% of tested months have p < 0.05 (chance alone would give 5%), though real surges explain part of that.

9.3 Is the detector well calibrated? The residual z¶

What to look at: the blue bars show how the detector's standardised residual z is actually distributed over all tested months. The black curve is the standard bell curve, which is what z would look like if the baseline were perfect. Right: same on a log scale to see the tails.

In plain words: the closer the blue bars follow the bell curve, the better calibrated the baseline. Blue bars sticking out on the right mean more big surprises than chance would produce, which is where real outbreaks and waves show up.

In [46]:
z = tt["z"]
bins = np.arange(-7.2, 7.41, 0.2)
xs = np.linspace(-7.2, 7.2, 400)

fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4))
for ax, log in ((a1, False), (a2, True)):
    ax.hist(z, bins=bins, density=True, color=BLUE, label="Observed (tested months)")
    ax.plot(xs, norm.pdf(xs), color=INK, lw=1.6, label="Standard bell curve")
    ax.set_xlabel("z (0 = as expected, +3 = very high)")
    ax.set_ylabel("Share of months (density)")
    if log:
        ax.set_yscale("log")
        ax.set_ylim(1e-5, 1)
        ax.set_title("Same, log scale (shows the tails)")
    else:
        ax.set_title("Residuals vs the ideal bell curve")
        ax.legend(loc="upper right")
fig.tight_layout()
save_chart(fig, "9_3_is_the_detector_well_calibrated_the_residual_z.png")
plt.show()

above, below = (z > 3).mean(), (z < -3).mean()
display(
    Markdown(
        f"**Takeaway:** the middle of the distribution is close to the bell curve, but the right tail is much heavier: {above:.1%} of months have z above +3, "
        f"versus {below:.1%} below -3 (a perfect bell curve gives 0.13% each). Mean z is {z.mean():.2f} and the spread {z.std():.2f} (ideal 0 and 1). "
        "So the baseline is easily surprised on the upside: its biggest surprises are real outbreak waves, but expect some false alarms too."
    )
)

Takeaway: the middle of the distribution is close to the bell curve, but the right tail is much heavier: 4.8% of months have z above +3, versus 0.4% below -3 (a perfect bell curve gives 0.13% each). Mean z is 0.23 and the spread 1.52 (ideal 0 and 1). So the baseline is easily surprised on the upside: its biggest surprises are real outbreak waves, but expect some false alarms too.

9.4 Baseline vs autoregressive detector: alerts per year¶

What to look at: two bars per year. Blue is the baseline (tests_outbreaks); orange is the variant that also uses last month's count (tests_outbreaks_ar1). Both test exactly the same series-months; only tested rows are counted. The pale bars are 2026 (partial year).

In [47]:
ar1 = pd.read_parquet(C.PROCESSED / "tests_outbreaks_ar1.parquet")
t_ar = ar1[ar1["status"] == "tested"]


def alert_episodes(d):
    """Alert months, and episodes (runs of consecutive alert months within one series)."""
    a = d[d["alert"]].sort_values(["level", "disease", "area", "month"])
    key = a[["level", "disease", "area"]]
    mnum = a["month"].dt.year * 12 + a["month"].dt.month
    new = key.ne(key.shift()).any(axis=1) | (mnum.diff() != 1)
    return len(a), int(new.sum())


n_b, ep_b = alert_episodes(tt)
n_a, ep_a = alert_episodes(t_ar)
by_year = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "Baseline": tt.groupby(tt["month"].dt.year)["alert"].sum(),
        "Autoregressive": t_ar.groupby(t_ar["month"].dt.year)["alert"].sum(),
    }
)
x, w = by_year.index.to_numpy(), 0.38

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 4.2))
ax.bar(
    x - w / 2,
    by_year["Baseline"],
    width=w,
    color=[BLUE_LIGHT if v == 2026 else BLUE for v in x],
    label="Baseline",
)
ax.bar(
    x + w / 2,
    by_year["Autoregressive"],
    width=w,
    color=[ORANGE_LIGHT if v == 2026 else ORANGE for v in x],
    label="Autoregressive (also uses last month)",
)
ax.set_xticks(x[::2])
ax.set_xlabel("Year")
ax.set_ylabel("Alert months")
ax.set_title("Alerts per year, two detector variants")
ax.legend(loc="upper left")
fig.tight_layout()
save_chart(fig, "9_4_baseline_vs_autoregressive_alerts_per_year.png")
plt.show()

display(
    Markdown(
        f"**Takeaway:** the autoregressive variant raises {n_a:,} alerts against {n_b:,} for the baseline, grouped into {ep_a:,} and {ep_b:,} episodes "
        f"(runs of consecutive alert months), so an average episode lasts {n_a / ep_a:.1f} months instead of {n_b / ep_b:.1f}. "
        "The baseline keeps a whole wave flagged; the autoregressive variant flags shorter bursts, because it asks whether a month is a surprise given last month."
    )
)

Takeaway: the autoregressive variant raises 1,740 alerts against 2,210 for the baseline, grouped into 1,028 and 980 episodes (runs of consecutive alert months), so an average episode lasts 1.7 months instead of 2.3. The baseline keeps a whole wave flagged; the autoregressive variant flags shorter bursts, because it asks whether a month is a surprise given last month.

10. Things worth knowing before modelling¶

(Numbers below are computed from the data above each time the notebook runs.)

display(Markdown("\n".join("- " + b for b in bullets)))
  • Volume grows over time (events x8, outbreaks x25 between 2005 and 2025). Trends in raw counts mix disease spread with better reporting.
  • Three diseases and one region dominate (African swine fever virus, HPAI (all hosts) and Bluetongue virus are 76% of outbreaks; Europe is 71%).
  • The newest months are incomplete because reports arrive late (median 15 days, 90th percentile 104 days, the longest 5.8 years). Only 1 outbreak starts in July 2026.
  • Odd dates: 296 outbreaks were reported before they started (negative lag), and 2,188 more than a year after.
  • Animal counts are patchy: 52% of outbreaks have susceptible = 0 (probably 'not reported'), 22,638 have cases = 0, and dead is bigger than cases in 2,809. Treat these columns with caution.
  • 20% of coordinates are approximate, which matters little for an 18 km weather cell but does matter for fine-scale analysis.
  • Antarctica is the only Other region (2 outbreaks) and is excluded from the detector.
  • Possible duplicates: 4,376 rows share disease, coordinates and start date with another row; this can be genuine (several farms reported at one point).
  • Weather quirks: 1.5% of prec_z values are exactly 0 (desert months where rain never varies); 17 rows have tmax slightly below tmin.
  • Weather stops in Dec 2024. Disease data after that cannot be matched with weather, so it serves as a holdout.
  • The outbreak detector is sensitive: 2,210 alerts in 45,242 tested months (4.9%); 10% of tested months have p < 0.05 (chance gives 5%) and z has mean 0.23 and spread 1.52 (ideal 0 and 1); 378 months (0.8%) sit at the +7 cap. The autoregressive variant is calmer (1,740 alerts, shorter episodes).
  • The event detector is quiet: only 26 alerts in 27,600 tested event-months.
